name: read
content:
1	In recent years, researchers and public health programs and practices have focused on preventing,
     2	managing, and controlling traditional CVD risk factors by instituting timely intervention programs,
     3	identifying social determinants of health (SDOH), examining disparities in CVD risks, assessing the
     4	COVID-19 pandemic’s impact on CVD risks, and implementing collective efforts through community-based
     5	approaches to achieve population-level improvements in cardiovascular health. This special PCD
     6	collection of 20 articles published from January 2020 through November 2022 highlights some of these
     7	efforts by using multiple data sources collected before or during the pandemic. For instance,
     8	cigarette smoking and risk-enhancing factors related to pregnancy have been shown to increase CVD
     9	risks with significant implications (eg, increased infant mortality). Disparities in hypertension,
    10	stroke, and stroke mortality exist, exhibiting significant sociodemographic (eg, racial) and
    11	geographic (eg, rural–urban, county, zip code) variations. Intervention programs, such as behavioral
    12	modifications strengthening chronic disease awareness, use of self-measured blood pressure
    13	monitoring, and sodium intake reduction, are evaluated. The impact of COVID-19 on CVD is also
    14	explored. Finally, systematic reviews and meta-analyses evaluated the associations of circulating
    15	vitamin D levels, vitamin D supplementation, or high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) with
    16	blood pressure or stroke. These 20 articles advance our understanding of effective CVD risk
    17	management and intervention programs in multiple settings — in the general population and among
    18	high-risk groups — with a health equity lens across 3 broad themes further explored in this essay:
    19	
    20	
    21	 Examining factors contributing to CVD risk
    22	 Exploring factors contributing to disparities in CVD
    23	 Using community-based approaches to decrease CVDExamining the Factors Contributing to CVD Risk
    24	 The greatest contributors to CVD-related years of life lost globally are tobacco exposure,
    25	hypertension, high body mass index (BMI), and high fasting plasma glucose (3). Tobacco exposure,
    26	including cigarette smoking, secondhand smoke, and use of smokeless tobacco, contributed to 8.7
    27	million deaths worldwide in 2019, one-third of which were due to CVD (3). Hypertension affects more
    28	than 4 billion people worldwide, representing a near doubling in the absolute prevalence of
    29	hypertension since 1990 (3). In the US, nearly half of adults (47%) have hypertension, but only
    30	about 1 in 4 (24%) have their condition under control (7). Elevated BMI continues to increase
    31	globally, with significant effects on death, disability, and quality of life (3). The prevalence of
    32	obesity has increased worldwide in the past 50 years, reaching pandemic levels. Obesity represents a
    33	major health challenge because it substantially increases the risk of diseases such as hypertension,
    34	myocardial infarction, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and dementia, thereby contributing to a decline in
    35	both quality of life and life expectancy (8). Furthermore, global increases in high fasting plasma
    36	glucose and its sequelae, type 2 diabetes, have mirrored the increases seen in BMI over the past 3
    37	decades (9). Other behavioral risks (eg, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, inadequate sleep,
    38	excessive alcohol use); environmental risks (eg, air pollution, extreme temperatures); and social
    39	risks (eg, house and food insecurity) also contribute to increased CVD burden and disparities in
    40	cardiovascular morbidity and mortality (10)
    41	 Several of the contextual risk factors attributed to increased CVD burden are covered in this
    42	special collection. Cigarette smoking persists among adults with chronic disease. Using data from
    43	the 2019 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), Loretan and colleagues reported that more than 1
    44	in 4 US adults aged 18 to 64 years with 1 or more chronic diseases associated with smoking were
    45	current smokers (11). The current cigarette smoking prevalence in the US reached 51.9% among adults
    46	aged 18 to 44 years with 2 or more chronic diseases (11). Furthermore, that study showed that
    47	smoking cessation services were not being provided to almost 1 in 3 people who have a chronic
    48	disease, leaving important steps to be taken toward successful smoking cessation in this population
    49	(11). Also concerning, rates of smoking vary significantly across countries, and approximately 1
    50	billion people smoke globally, with significant negative implications for cardiovascular health (3).
    51	Goulding and colleagues used National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data collected from
    52	2011 through 2018 to provide estimates of the prevalence of high blood pressure among US children
    53	aged 8 to 17 years. The authors documented that elevated blood pressure was most prevalent among
    54	children who were older, male, or non-Hispanic Black, with factors beyond inequalities in body
    55	weight likely contributing to disparities in elevated blood pressure (12). Furthermore, a
    56	meta-analysis conducted by Qie and colleagues determined that a high level of HDL-C may provide a
    57	protective effect on the risk of total stroke and ischemic stroke but may increase the risk of
    58	intracerebral hemorrhage (13). Another meta-analysis by Zhang and colleagues found an L-shaped
    59	dose–response relationship between circulating vitamin D levels and the risk of hypertension;
    60	however, the pooled results of randomized controlled trials did not show vitamin D supplementation
    61	to be effective in preventing hypertension (14).
    62	 Studies in this collection also identified populations and communities with higher prevalence or at
    63	higher risk for CVD. In a cross-sectional study using 2018 NHIS data, Mendez and colleagues
    64	documented a higher prevalence of CVD and its risk factors among US adults with vision impairment
    65	(15). Salahuddin and colleagues documented zip code variations in infant mortality rates associated
    66	with a high prevalence of maternal cardiometabolic high-risk conditions (chronic or gestational
    67	diabetes, chronic or gestational hypertension, smoking during pregnancy, and prepregnancy obesity)
    68	in 2 counties in Texas (16). Findings from these articles could direct efforts to implement
    69	appropriate strategies to prevent, manage, and control CVD in populations at high risk.
    70	 Top
    71	 Exploring Factors Contributing to Disparities in CVD
    72	 CVD and its related risk factors are increasingly recognized as growing indicators of global health
    73	disparities (17). Globally, differences in morbidity and mortality from CVD exist among high-,
    74	middle-, and low-income countries and across ethnic groups (1,3,5,6,17,18). In the US, disparities
    75	in CVD morbidity, mortality, and risk factors have persisted for decades, with concerning stagnation
    76	and significant upward trends since the early 2000s (18). Disparities are largely influenced by
    77	demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental factors (19,20). For example, African American and
    78	American Indian adults experience a higher burden of cardiovascular risk factors and CVD compared
    79	with non-Hispanic White adults (18). Unfortunately, structural racism remains a significant cause of
    80	poor cardiovascular health, restricting racial and ethnic minority populations from opportunities to
    81	live healthier lives, in healthier neighborhoods, and from access to quality education and health
    82	care (20).

The article, part of a special collection of 20 articles published from January 2020 through November 2022, discusses hypertension as a major cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factor with significant global and national implications. The collection highlights efforts to prevent, manage, and control traditional CVD risk factors by instituting timely intervention programs, identifying social determinants of health, examining disparities in CVD risks, and implementing community-based approaches to achieve population-level improvements in cardiovascular health.

Globally, hypertension affects more than 4 billion people, representing a near doubling in the absolute prevalence of hypertension since 1990. In the United States, nearly half of adults (47%) have hypertension, but only about 1 in 4 (24%) have their condition under control. The article identifies hypertension, along with tobacco exposure, high body mass index, and high fasting plasma glucose, as one of the greatest contributors to CVD-related years of life lost worldwide.

The article highlights that disparities in hypertension exist, exhibiting significant sociodemographic variations, such as racial differences, and geographic variations, including rural–urban differences, county-level differences, and zip code-level differences. These disparities are part of a broader pattern of CVD disparities that have persisted for decades in the US, with concerning stagnation and significant upward trends since the early 2000s. Disparities are largely influenced by demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental factors.

Regarding intervention programs, the article notes that behavioral modifications strengthening chronic disease awareness, use of self-measured blood pressure monitoring, and sodium intake reduction are evaluated as strategies to manage and control hypertension and other CVD risk factors.

The article also references a study by Goulding and colleagues that used National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data collected from 2011 through 2018 to provide estimates of the prevalence of high blood pressure among US children aged 8 to 17 years. The authors documented that elevated blood pressure was most prevalent among children who were older, male, or non-Hispanic Black, with factors beyond inequalities in body weight likely contributing to disparities in elevated blood pressure.

Additionally, the article mentions a study by Salahuddin and colleagues that documented zip code variations in infant mortality rates associated with a high prevalence of maternal cardiometabolic high-risk conditions, including chronic or gestational hypertension, in 2 counties in Texas.

Overall, the article positions hypertension as a critical public health concern requiring sustained, multifaceted intervention efforts across diverse populations and settings.
